morning_soundtrack.title: John Prine on music, cancer and why he never thought he'd be a recording artist
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Prine died in 2020 from complications of COVID-19. To mark what would have been his 80th birthday, we listen to an interview from 2018 in which he talked about the surgeries that altered his voice.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The bittersweet ache of a voice you'll never hear new again, celebrated on a birthday that will never come.

morning_soundtrack.title: The Decemberists Share New Song From Movie Adaptation Of Colin Meloy’s Wildwood
morning_soundtrack.snippet: If you've navigated your web browser to stereogum dot com today, you likely know Colin Meloy first and foremost as the frontman for longstanding bookish indie-folk greats the Decemberists. But for a segment of the population, Meloy is best known as the author of the Wildwood Chronicles, a series of fantasy novels aimed at teens and preteens, set in his native Portland and illustrated by his wife Carson Ellis. (We talked to him about it in our We've Got A File On You interview.) Wildwood , the first of those books, has been adapted into a stop-motion animated movie, and unsurprisingly, the Decemberists are on the soundtrack.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Misty forest paths and dog-eared paperbacks, scored by people who clearly still believe in magic.

morning_soundtrack.title: Alanis Morissette Announces New Christmas Album Feat. Brandi Carlile, Steve Martin, & Martin Short
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Alanis Morissette is here to remind you of the Christ- mess that you left when you went away. Look, you try to come up with a better pun. Go ahead.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Eggnog spiked with irony, served at a holiday party where someone's definitely about to say something uncomfortable.

morning_soundtrack.title: boygenius Reunite For Phoebe Bridgers’ Lance Oppenheim-Directed Acoustic Performance
morning_soundtrack.snippet: According to every review that I've read, Phoebe Bridgers is putting in some amazing performances on her current arena tour. But unless you go see the show for yourself, you have to rely on secondhand accounts. Bridgers famously banned phones from those shows, which means there's basically no footage out there.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The rare, hushed intimacy of a performance that feels like it was never meant for you — and is somehow better for it.

morning_soundtrack.title: BONUS TRACKS: A Coda for a Tour Manager and This Week’s Roots Music News
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Too often lately, I’ve been writing about artists who have passed — Dolly Parton , Glen Hansard , Cassandra Wilson , and Raul Malo . But I want to dedicate this week’s column to those who worked tirelessly behind the scenes, so that musicians like them and others could perform
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A quiet backstage grief, the kind that smells like road cases and old laminate passes.

morning_soundtrack.title: ALBUM REVIEW: Todd Snider's Posthumous 'My Second Rodeo' Is a Poignant Reminder of What We've Lost
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The last memory some fans have of the late Todd Snider is his singing and dancing with Margo Price on the Ryman stage at last year's John Prine "You Got Gold" celebration in Nashville. Snider had a unique stage presence — usually barefoot, his face lit
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Barefoot on a wooden stage, grinning through the last song — a warmth that makes the silence after it unbearable.

morning_soundtrack.title: The Decemberists Premiere First Song in Two Years
morning_soundtrack.snippet: “The Better Part of Bravery” was made for Wildwood, a film based on Colin Meloy’s debut novel
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Stepping back into a beloved, overgrown garden after years away and finding it exactly as strange and beautiful as you remembered.

morning_soundtrack.title: Alanis Morissette Made a Holiday Album
morning_soundtrack.snippet: This Christmas season, expect Good Weather for Immaculate Conception
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Christmas morning filtered through someone who's processed a lot of feelings since last December.

morning_soundtrack.title: Watch Phoebe Bridgers and Boygenius Perform Live in New Short Film
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Bridgers is the latest guest on A24’s Sound Check at Cherry Lane Theatre YouTube series
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Three friends in a candlelit room, playing like the arena tour never happened and the whole world fits in one microphone.

morning_soundtrack.title: The Wicker Man (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Part folk record, part pagan fever dream, The Wicker Man’s soundtrack is so steeped in sex, fertility, ritual and ancient melody that listening to it feels like stumbling upon something unearthed rather than recorded. Paul Giovanni’s songs create a world that feels simultaneously ancient and entirely invented—warm, earthy, erotic and communal, and perhaps all the more unsettling for sounding so beautiful. The post The Wicker Man (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack) first appeared on Aquarium Drunkard .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Music that feels like it was dug out of the earth at dusk, still warm and smelling faintly of something you can't name.

morning_soundtrack.title: The Decemberists Return with New Song “The Better Part of Bravery”: Stream
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Written for the animated stop-motion film Wildwood, based on frontman Colin Meloy's debut novel. The Decemberists Return with New Song “The Better Part of Bravery”: Stream Eddie Fu
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The opening chapter of an adventure told in minor keys and wool coats, somewhere between a map and a lullaby.

morning_soundtrack.title: Isaac Slade Joins Ed Sheeran’s Tour as New Opening Act
morning_soundtrack.snippet: After Sheeran's previous openers dropped off the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Isaac Slade Joins Ed Sheeran’s Tour as New Opening Act Alex Young
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The musical equivalent of a last-minute substitute teacher — fine, probably fine, everyone's just a little unsettled.

global_silver_linings.title: NPR-Inspired Homework Leads Teen to Find Hidden Message a Decade After a Stranger’s Kindness
global_silver_linings.snippet: From Seattle’s chapter of National Public Radio comes the remarkable story of the kindness of strangers immortalized in an origami crane. Published through KUOW’s “My Unsung Hero” series, the story begins with a 7-year-old in Japan who had just gotten a new bike. Young Rika Matsuda was at first very excited because the bike was […]
global_silver_linings.reason: A small act of kindness planted a seed that quietly grew for a decade, and one curious teenager's homework assignment brought it back to light — proof that generosity leaves a longer trail than we ever know.

global_silver_linings.title: ‘I can breathe again’. Readers share their experiences of a more balanced media diet
global_silver_linings.snippet: We often talk about the impact journalism has on democracy and how we understand the world. But what about its impact on how we feel?
global_silver_linings.reason: Readers are actively choosing how they consume news and reporting feeling lighter and more grounded for it — a quiet but powerful reminder that we have more agency over our mental landscape than the algorithm would have us believe.

global_silver_linings.title: 22 teachers share the moment they realized they had a child genius in their classroom
global_silver_linings.snippet: "I had one student who literally memorized the English dictionary, and English was their second language."
global_silver_linings.reason: Teachers on the front lines of the classroom are still having those electric moments of recognising extraordinary potential in young people — a heartening sign that curiosity and brilliance keep showing up, in every kind of kid, every year.

global_silver_linings.title: Podcast Transcript October 9th, 2026— (Guest Interview) A place to breathe: inside #CreateConnectCare, the youth mental health program giving young people a voice | World Mental Health Day 2026
global_silver_linings.snippet: Episode Description: If you have a teenager in your life and you’ve felt them pull away from conversations you used to have easily, this episode is for you. Kathy Saulitis has spent three years going through what young people write and create when nobody is grading it: the poems, drawings, essays, and songs submitted to […] The post Podcast Transcript October 9th, 2026— (Guest Interview) A place to breathe: inside #CreateConnectCare, the youth mental health program giving young people a voice | World Mental Health Day 2026 first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: A dedicated mental health programme is handing young people a microphone rather than a prescription, letting them shape the conversation about their own wellbeing — exactly the kind of youth-led, human-centred approach that builds lasting resilience.

discovery_articles.title: High Shoals Falls  in Hiawassee, Georgia
discovery_articles.snippet: High Shoals Falls is a secluded waterfall. To get there you must access the trailhead on Indian Grave Gap Rd in Hiawassee, Ga. The drive up the mountain is exhilarating.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: High Shoals Falls earns its seclusion — tucked into the North Georgia mountains along a road whose name, Indian Grave Gap, hints at histories far older than any trail marker. Some places reward you simply for showing up willing.

discovery_articles.title: Tiptree Jam Museum in Tiptree, England
discovery_articles.snippet: If you have stayed in hotels in the UK, you likely got a mini jam from Wilkin & Sons at your breakfast buffet. In a converted barn on the grounds of the Wilkin & Sons preserve factory in an Essex village, the Tiptree Jam Museum tells the story of one of Britain's most beloved jam brands. The entrance is marked by a long, retro-looking pole which was in fact the Tiptree Jam Factory's chimney from 1984 to 2021.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The Tiptree Jam Museum's entrance marker is the factory's old chimney, quietly repurposed into a retro landmark after nearly four decades of belching smoke — a very British kind of monument. There's something endearing about a nation that builds shrines to its breakfast spreads.

discovery_articles.title: Gold Rush Cabin in Dawson City, Yukon
discovery_articles.snippet: No one knows exactly when Dawson City's Gold Rush Cabin was built, but historical records place it here by 1900 and suggest it may be somewhat older. Its earliest documented connections are to the Trading & Exploring Company, one of the businesses operating in Dawson as the frenzy of the Klondike Gold Rush was beginning to subside. Somehow, the little log cabin survived what happened next.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A nameless cabin that nobody can quite date, tied to a gold rush already burning itself out, and it 'somehow survived what happened next' — which is exactly the kind of sentence that demands you find out what happened next. Dawson City's past is stranger than most fiction.

discovery_articles.title: This One-of-a-Kind Bronze Ring Offers a Tantalizing Glimpse at the Lighthouse of Alexandria, a Lost Wonder of the Ancient World
discovery_articles.snippet: Archaeologists in Egypt discovered the signet ring while conducting excavations on the island of Antirhodos, which once housed a lavish Ptolemaic palace
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A small bronze signet ring, pulled from the seafloor off Alexandria, may carry the only surviving portrait of the ancient world's most famous lighthouse — a wonder so thoroughly lost that this tiny band is now among our best evidence it existed at all.

discovery_articles.title: A Community-Led Archaeology Dig on a Tiny Scottish Isle Has Unearthed a Medieval Monastery of 'International Importance'
discovery_articles.snippet: The settlement, founded by an early Christian saint in the 500s, is "far more than a small island church." It may have played a larger role in the Christianization of Britain than historians once realized
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A community dig on a remote Scottish isle has quietly redrawn the map of early Christianity in Britain, suggesting a sixth-century saint's modest settlement did far more missionary heavy lifting than anyone had credited. History, it turns out, was hiding on a small island the whole time.

discovery_articles.title: Could This Dutch Invention Help Tackle Plastic Pollution in America's Waterways?
discovery_articles.snippet: The Netherlands has had success with the Bubble Barrier, which pumps air bubbles from the bottom of a canal or river to direct plastic to the surface. Now, Lansing, Michigan, is looking to be the first to install the technology stateside
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The Bubble Barrier works by doing something almost absurdly simple — blowing air bubbles from a riverbed to herd floating plastic to the surface — and yet it's genuinely effective, which makes you wonder why we reach for complexity first. Lansing, Michigan, is about to find out if elegant Dutch logic translates across the Atlantic.

discovery_articles.title: Scientists Took a Cheek Swab From the World's Oldest Tortoise. His DNA Could Reveal Hints to Longevity
discovery_articles.snippet: Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise, is about 194 years old and the oldest land animal alive today. Discoveries about his genetics could provide clues to extending lifespan in humans
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Jonathan the tortoise was already middle-aged when Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species,' and now scientists are reading his DNA for clues to why some creatures simply refuse to age at the usual pace. There's something humbling about taking longevity lessons from an animal that has outlived every human who has ever cared for him.

discovery_articles.title: How the Grand Canyon could have lost 1 billion years of geologic history
discovery_articles.snippet: The rise and fall of a continent-spanning cliff may help explain a mysterious 1-billion-year gap in Earth’s geologic history, a new study suggests.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A billion years of Earth's story just vanishes inside the Grand Canyon's rock layers — not lost to erosion alone, but possibly erased by a continent-wide cliff that rose and fell like a slow, geological exhale. The canyon we visit for its grandeur is also, quietly, a crime scene.

discovery_articles.title: Here’s a look at the Nobel Prizes for science
discovery_articles.snippet: An icy window into the cosmos, a light switch for the brain and solving the mystery of mirror image molecules all took home the top prize.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A light switch for the brain, an icy cosmic window, and the riddle of mirror-image molecules — this year's Nobel science prizes read less like a syllabus and more like the opening chapters of three different science fiction novels, all of them true.

discovery_articles.title: How to Keep Track of Your Sources on JSTOR
discovery_articles.snippet: Learn where to find bibliographic information so you have the details you need when it’s time to cite your research.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A practical guide to citing your JSTOR sources — useful, thorough, and about as surprising as a stapler. Keep it bookmarked; you'll want it eventually.

discovery_articles.title: How Does Life Unfold? A Landscape Metaphor Comes Into Its Own.
discovery_articles.snippet: C.H. Waddington’s powerful image of embryonic stem cells specializing on a rolling landscape has captivated biologists since the 1950s. Experimental data is finally confirming, and complicating, his visionary ideas. The post How Does Life Unfold?
discovery_articles.ferns_note: In the 1950s, biologist C.H. Waddington sketched a rolling landscape of hills and valleys to explain how a single cell 'decides' what kind of cell to become — a metaphor so evocative it outlasted the science it was meant to illustrate. Decades later, experimental data is finally catching up, and the landscape turns out to be far messier, and more interesting, than he imagined.

discovery_articles.title: Jonathan Knight’s Meditative Series ‘Exhale’ Invites Us to Slow Down and Practice Noticing
discovery_articles.snippet: Knight conceived of 'Exhale' as a way to explore the nuances of color and "the emotional experience of looking."
discovery_articles.ferns_note: 'Exhale' asks you to do something photography rarely demands: not to look at the subject, but to sit with the act of looking itself. Jonathan Knight's meditative color studies are the visual equivalent of being told, gently, to put your phone down.

discovery_articles.title: Symmetry Meets the Sacred in Shuling Guo’s Dreamy, Diffused Paintings
discovery_articles.snippet: Guo's paintings in 'Temple II,' opening next week at Hollis Taggart, explore memory, presence, and loss.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Shuling Guo layers temple architecture with personal memory until the two blur into something that feels sacred and half-forgotten at once — paintings that locate loss not in absence, but in the soft edges of what almost remains. 'Temple II' opens next week, and it sounds like the kind of show that follows you home.

featured_read.title: See the Artemis II Crew’s Handwritten Notes Documenting the Lunar Surface
featured_read.snippet: People like to say we have more computing power in our pockets than NASA used to get to the moon, but even that understates things. The Apollo guidance computer had a measly four kilobytes of RAM, while the iPhone 17 Pro Max has 12 gigabytes—an increase of roughly three million-fold. Of course the Artemis II astronauts who visited the moon earlier this year had state-of-the-art technology, not just housed in the vehicle, but in their pockets as well.
featured_read.blurb: When the Artemis II astronauts reached the lunar surface, they reached for something surprisingly analog — and their handwritten notes reveal what state-of-the-art technology still can't capture about the act of witnessing. A quiet meditation on observation, documentation, and what it means to be a human hand at the edge of the universe.

reading_room.title: Why moving on after a breakup makes you a better person
reading_room.snippet: They say time heals a broken heart. But do the hard work of moving on, and you do more than heal – you improve yourself - by Matthew Barnfield Read on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: Moving on from a breakup turns out to be less about forgetting and more about the surprisingly rigorous work of rebuilding a self — Matthew Barnfield makes a careful case that heartbreak, if you let it, is one of the most effective instruments of genuine growth we have.

reading_room.title: Passages We Underlined This Fall
reading_room.snippet: A selection of some of our favorite passages from September and October new releases.
reading_room.blurb: The Paris Review gathered the sentences that stopped their editors cold this fall — not reviews, not recommendations, just the raw moments where language did something unexpected. A lovely way to find your next book through someone else's margin notes.

reading_room.title: Up a Creek
reading_room.snippet: "Nature writing after everyone stopped paying attention."
reading_room.blurb: Written in the key of quiet defiance, this essay asks what it means to pay attention to the natural world precisely when collective attention has moved on entirely. Nature writing as an act of almost stubborn love.

reading_room.title: Lit Hub Daily: October 9, 2026
reading_room.snippet: Morgan Entrekin attends the Heinrich Maria Ledig-Rowohlt Translation Prize dinner at the Frankfurt Book Fair. | Lit Hub On Translation Demetris Papadimitropoulos considers the complex relationships between queer people and their families through reading Families We Keep and Families We
reading_room.blurb: Through two books about chosen and unchosen families, Demetris Papadimitropoulos traces the particular tension queer people navigate between the families they were given and the ones they build — a reading that doubles as a meditation on loyalty, loss, and what we owe each other.

reading_room.title: We Are Already Post-Human
reading_room.blurb: The provocative claim here isn't that we're becoming post-human — it's that we already are, and have been for longer than we'd like to admit. A piece that quietly dismantles the line we draw between ourselves and our tools.
